Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify common tendinopathies of the hand and wrist.
Explain the epidemiology and pathophysiology of common tendinopathies of the hand and
wrist.
Describe the physical examination and specific tests to diagnose common tendinopathies of
the hand and wrist.
List treatment options for common tendinopathies of the hand and wrist.
Introduction
The most common symptomatic tendinopathies of the hand and wrist for which individuals
seek specialty care are trigger digit and de Quervain tendinopathy.

Less common tendinopathies of the hand and wrist include flexor carpi radialis (FCR)
tendinopathy, extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendinopathy, and extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)
tendinopathy.
General Considerations
Many tendinopathies occur at sites at which the tendon passes through a tunnel or sheath.
No known cause (idiopathic) of tunnel tendinopathies exists.
The pathology is mucoid degeneration and fibrocartilaginous metaplasia1
Pain and tenderness are discrete.
Provocative testing may be characteristic.
Imaging studies are uncommonly used for diagnosis because symptoms and signs are
characteristic.
The natural history often is self-limiting.
Hand and wrist tendinopathies may resolve with no specific management. For example,
evidence suggests that de Quervain tendinopathy generally is self-limiting. The high incidence
of incidental ECU and FCR tendinopathies observed on imaging studies obtained for reasons
other than pain suggests that these tendinopathies may cause symptoms for a limited time.
Trigger digit, particularly mild trigger digit, often resolves without management.
Nonspecific symptom alleviation: splints, NSAIDs (oral or topical), acetaminophen, ice/heat
Corticosteroid injection may be disease-modifying for trigger digit; however, it is not clearly
better than a placebo injection at other sites.
Surgical management involves opening/cutting the sheath/tunnel that the tendon passes
through.
Idiopathic Trigger Digit
Also known as stenosing tenosynovitis of the flexor tendons
The characteristic physical examination finding is catching or locking with flexion (tight fist in
particular), tenderness and a bump at the A1 pulley, and often a slight proximal
interphalangeal joint flexion contracture (Figure 1)
The flexor digitorum profundus tendon is enlarged, whereas the flexor digitorum superficialis
(FDS) often is unaffected.
Idiopathic trigger digit is common. No clear associations exist with other conditions.

Idiopathic Trigger Digit
The proposed association of trigger finger with diabetes mellitus is not proven
experimentally. Both conditions are common, and whether their pathophysiologies are
related is unknown. Biologically, endocrinopathy may be related to trigger digit. The
following comorbidities for trigger digit often are listed without experimental evidence:
hypothyroidism, sarcoidosis, gout, calcific tendinitis, pseudogout, and amyloidosis.
Epidemiology
The lifetime prevalence of trigger finger is unknown.
Women are more likely to present for treatment than men.2 The age distribution is bimodal,
including peaks among children younger than 8 years (mostly thumbs) and adults aged 40 to
60 years.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Tenderness to palpation of the flexor tendon at the level of the A1 pulley
Patients with trigger finger often experience painful catching of the finger with attempted
finger flexion.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients have tenderness to palpation in the volar aspect of the hand over the A1 pulley
of the affected finger. A palpable nodule may be observed on the tendon near the A1
pulley that moves as the tendon moves. A small, firm nodule over the A1 pulley that
does not move with tendon motion may be a retinacular ganglion cyst. Active firm flexion
of all the fingers into a tight fist despite the pain, with subsequent extension of the
fingers, will demonstrate triggering. The condition ranges from mild uneven movement to
difficulty prying the finger out of flexion.
Green categorized trigger digits as follows:3
Grade I: isolated pain over the A1 pulley
Grade II: uneven movement of the finger
Grade III: locking of the finger in flexion that is passively correctable
Grade IV: fixed, locked finger
Quinnell4 graded trigger digits as follows:
Grade 0: normal movement of the digit (possible trigger digit)
Grade 1: uneven movement
Grade 2: actively correctable locking of the digit
Grade 3: passively correctible locking of the digit
Grade 4: fixed deformity
Pain over the A1 pulley and the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint is not in itself
diagnostic of trigger finger. Elderly patients may have symptoms of pain in this area with
a sensation of locking of the digit. The locking sensation may be related to joint stiffness

because of osteoarthritis and must not be misdiagnosed as trigger finger because
management for trigger finger is not the same as management for MCP osteoarthritis.
The differential diagnosis for a patient with pain at the level of the MCP joint and
subjective tendon symptoms also includes sagittal band insufficiency with subluxation of
the extensor apparatus. This diagnosis may be a long-standing issue related to tissue
laxity or rheumatoid arthritis or occur acutely (eg, sagittal band rupture).
Imaging Studies
Imaging studies do not aid in the diagnosis of trigger digit.
Enlargement of the tendon can be observed on ultrasonographic images and MRIs.
Management
More than one-half of patients who do not have insulin-requiring diabetes mellitus experience
resolution of triggering via one or two corticosteroid injections.

Management
Patients with diabetes mellitus may not benefit from a second corticosteroid injection as
much as patients without diabetes mellitus.5 Patients with diabetes mellitus who take
insulin can be counseled that they likely will experience hyperglycemia (30% to 50%
increase in glucose level) for more than 1 week after injection (for this condition and
others).
Surgical release of the A1 Pulley
The surgical approach for A1 pulley release involves a transverse, oblique, or longitudinal
incision over the A1 pulley at the level of the metacarpal head of the involved finger
(Video 1; Figure 2). In surgical release for trigger thumb, the radial digital nerve is
relatively superficial and vulnerable as it passes over the radial sesamoid. A tight band of
tissue may be present just proximal to the A1 pulley, occasionally called the A0 or
oblique pulley, and triggering occasionally persists after the A1 pulley is released if this

In pediatric patients, trigger digits other than the thumb are uncommon. Multiple trigger
digits in pediatric patients may be associated with mucopolysaccharidoses, and
consideration frequently is given to the removal of one slip of the FDS tendon in this
setting. In pediatric patients without mucopolysaccharidoses, trigger digit may be
associated with anatomic differences of the FDS; these patients also may benefit from
removal of a slip of the FDS. Adult patients with long-standing triggering, a preexisting
proximal interphalangeal extensor lag, or poorly controlled diabetes mellitus also may
continue to experience triggering after A1 pulley release alone and may benefit from
excision of one slip of the FDS tendon, usually the ulnar slip. Finally, patients with a
trigger digit who have rheumatoid arthritis and ulnar drift of the digits at the MCP level
may be better treated via excision of one slip of the FDS rather than A1 pulley release. In
these patients, A1 pulley release may worsen ulnar drift.
Complications of open trigger finger release include infection, persistent triggering,
release of the A2 pulley leading to bowstringing, wound separation, synovial fistula,
tendon rupture, incomplete release, and (rarely) digital nerve injury.

de Quervain Tendinopathy
Tendinopathy of the first extensor compartment in the wrist
Patients have enlargement of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons
in the first extensor compartment.
The abductor pollicis longus tendon has wide variability in its insertions and the total number
of tendon slips present6
As much as 40% of the population has a separate subsheath for the extensor pollicis brevis
tendon. Inadequate surgical release of this separate subsheath may result in incomplete
symptom relief postoperatively.
Women present for treatment more often than men.
Peak incidence in adults aged 40 to 60 years.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Tenderness and enlargement over the radial styloid and the first dorsal extensor
compartment
Resisted radial abduction of the wrist may be painful.
Positive Finkelstein test—This test is performed by asking the patient to form a fist with the
thumb in the palm and with the forearm in neutral rotation. The examiner then passively
deviates the wrist in the ulnar direction. A positive test is indicated by pain over the first dorsal
compartment (Video 2).
Video 2 Seiler JG III: Physical examination of the hand and wrist: Special tests. Finkelstein test, in
Sarwark JF, ed: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2010, pp 404-415.
Management
Symptoms can be alleviated via NSAIDs/acetaminophen and splint immobilization.
In a study, 51% of patients reported improvement after one corticosteroid injection, and 73%
of patients reported improvement after a second injection; however, no experimental
evidence indicates that corticosteroid injections outperform simulated steroid injections.7

Whether corticosteroid injection is disease-modifying remains unclear (ie, whether the
duration of symptoms is shorter with the use of a steroid compared with a placebo injection
remains unclear).
In a database study, patients who underwent a corticosteroid injection were more likely to
undergo surgical treatment.8

Management
Surgical management involves release of the first extensor compartment (Video 3). The
anatomy of the first extensor compartment varies. In a cohort of 130 patients with de
Quervain tendinopathy who underwent surgical release, 37% had a single compartment,
55% had two subcompartments, and 8% had three subcompartments.6 Care must be
taken to release all compartments during surgical management. Potential complications
of surgical management include subluxation or dislocation of the tendons volarly and
injury of the superficial radial nerve.
Video 3 Roebke AJ, Jain SA, Mickley JP, Samade R: de Quervain Tenosynovitis Release With a
Chevron Incision [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020.

Intersection Syndrome
Acute, fast-resolving painful crepitation between the tendons of the first and second dorsal
compartments
Often associated with a recent period of greater than usual wrist motion, such as a weekend
canoeing excursion
Epidemiology
The prevalence of intersection syndrome is unknown because it resolves so rapidly that
patients may not seek formal medical care or specialty care. Regardless, intersection
syndrome is uncommonly seen in clinical practice.
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients who recently were more active with their wrist than usual (eg, on a weekend river
rowing trip) often note pain and squeaking in the wrist with motion.
Typically, palpable and audible crepitus is noted over the intersection of the first and second
extensor compartment regions as the wrist is flexed and extended.
Patients also may have localized tenderness 4 to 6 cm proximal to the Lister tubercle
corresponding to the anatomic crossing point of these compartments9
Management
NSAIDs and splint immobilization may alleviate pain.
Symptoms resolve in approximately 2 to 3 weeks.10 If symptoms persist more than a few
weeks, the diagnosis should be reconsidered.
Surgical management has been described but should be performed only in patients with
longer-lasting intersection syndrome; however, this is a subject of debate.10
EPL Tendinopathy

11/17

EPL tendinopathy is rare.
Commonly associated with nondisplaced distal radius fractures that are managed
nonsurgically.
Patients may have a prodromal period of wrist pain over the Lister tubercle with use of the
EPL, pain with passive extension of the interphalangeal joint over the Lister tubercle, and
weakness or pain with active extension of the thumb interphalangeal joint;11 however, this
pain may be difficult to discern during recovery from fracture.
May occur as long as 1 year after fracture
Patient History and Physical Examination
EPL tendinopathy usually is first noticed as rupture and loss of retropulsion of the thumb and
loss of interphalangeal joint hyperextension.
To identify EPL tendinopathy before rupture occurs, surgeons should assess for pain with
passive and active thumb interphalangeal joint extension.
The patient may have tenderness localized to the tendon near the Lister tubercle.
Patients may describe snapping with thumb extension.
Management
If a diagnosis of EPL tendinopathy is made before rupture, release or aspiration is
considered.12
After rupture, options are accommodation or tendon transfer, usually extensor indicis
proprius to EPL transfer.11
The surgical technique for prerupture management consists of release of the EPL tendon
within the third extensor compartment at the level of the Lister tubercle.13 The tendon is
transposed dorsoradially into the subcutaneous tissues.
Complications include damage to the branches of the superficial radial nerve and resultant
painful neuroma. No apparent differences in thumb mechanics have been described.
FCR Tendinopathy
FCR tendinopathy is thought to be associated with radiographic scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal
arthrosis; however, the source of pain may be difficult to distinguish.14

Patients may have pain and/or soft-tissue swelling over the FCR tendon region, particularly
with resisted wrist flexion.
This condition may complicate thumb carpometacarpal arthroplasty procedures in which
tendon transfer to the FCR or other manipulation of the FCR is performed.
Epidemiology
FCR tendinopathy is rare.
Incidence of FCR tendinopathy is increased individuals in their forties.14
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients have pain along the volar radial wrist at the level of the radiocarpal joint.
Physical examination findings include tenderness over the FCR tendon at the wrist flexion
crease and pain with resisted flexion and radial deviation of the wrist.
Management
NSAIDs, splint or brace immobilization, local corticosteroid injection
May be managed via surgical decompression if symptoms do not improve
Patients may experience spontaneous rupture that results in temporary pain and bruising;
however, resolution of pain and symptoms without impaired function after some time is
typical.
ECU Tendinopathy
ECU tendinopathy is a type of tunnel tendinopathy.
Often, a relatively straightforward diagnosis because of isolated tenderness over the ECU
tendon; however, proximity to the triangular fibrocartilage complex may make pathology in
this location part of the differential diagnosis.
Occasionally, this condition may include subluxation of the tendon ulnarly with wrist motion or
instability of the ECU in its groove.
Epidemiology
Common cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain

Occasionally, ECU tendinopathy is associated with subluxation of the tendon within its sheath;
however, a recent study of ECU subluxation observed on MRIs reported no correlation with
pain.15
Patient History and Physical Examination
Isolated tenderness of the ECU tendon
The ECU synergy test is a simple bedside physical examination maneuver that is reported to be
74% sensitive and 86% specific in diagnosis of ECU abnormalities observed on
ultrasonography.16

Patient History and Physical Examination
Sato et al16 compared the diagnostic utility of the ECU synergy test with
ultrasonographic examination of the ECU tendon in patients with chronic, ulnar-sided
wrist pain. Diagnosis of an ECU disorder was based on the ultrasonographic finding of
tendon sheath distension, Doppler flow within the tendon sheath, tendon enlargement,
or irregular internal echo texture. The synergy test is performed by asking the patient to
rest the elbow in 90° of flexion on the examination table. The examiner positions the
patient so that the fingers are extended and the dorsal hand faces the examiner. The
examiner grasps the patient’s thumb and long finger and asks the patient to deviate the
thumb radially against resistance. With the other hand, the examiner palpates the ECU
and FCU tendons at the wrist. The presence of pain suggests ECU tendon pathology.
Management
Typically, ECU tendinopathy will resolve with nonspecific palliative measures, such as NSAIDs
and immobilization.
Surgical management is discretionary and uncommon, and its role and benefits are unclear.
Multiple procedures and variations have been described.
